name: Strontium sulfide depilatory

lead: Strontium sulfide was one of several alkaline sulfide salts used in mid-twentieth-century depilatories, products that remove hair by chemically dissolving it rather than cutting it. The appearance payoff was smooth, hairless skin on legs, underarms or face without a razor.

It works by attacking the disulfide bonds that give hair its strength, leaving hair soft enough to wipe away. Published work on it is mostly mid-century: a German paper on how deep the effect reaches and a 1953 rat-skin study on depilation and the effect of lanolin afterwards.

paras: Sulfide depilatories were sold as powders mixed to a paste or as ready creams, spread over the area for a short time and then rinsed or scraped off. Results last until the hair regrows, typically days. Modern depilatories mostly use thioglycolate salts instead.

Strontium sulfide is classed as corrosive, can cause severe skin burns and eye damage, and releases hydrogen sulfide (a rotten-egg odour) with water. Chemical depilatories in general can cause irritation, burns and rashes, and product labels advise a patch test.

chain: Hair softens at the skin surface
Wiped away for a smooth, hairless look
angle.text: Applied as a paste or cream, the sulfide softens hair so it can be rinsed or scraped off, leaving smooth skin for days. It was one of the older chemical alternatives to shaving.

lead: Strontium sulfide (SrS) is an inorganic salt that was used as the active ingredient in some chemical depilatories, products that remove hair by dissolving it at the skin surface. Used on legs, underarms or face, it gave a smooth, hairless look that lasts until regrowth, without shaving.[1][2]

Chemical depilatories work by breaking the disulfide bonds in keratin, the protein that gives hair its strength, so the hair softens and can be wiped off. Their effect is temporary, lasting from hours to days.[3]

Research on strontium sulfide depilation is largely from the mid-twentieth century. A 1952 German-language study examined the depth effect of strontium sulfide depilatories, and a 1953 laboratory study looked at strontium sulfide depilation of rat skin and the effect of lanolin on the depilated skin.[4][1] Strontium sulfide itself is a corrosive industrial intermediate produced by heating celestite with coke.[2]
infobox: Heating celestite (strontium sulfate) with coke at about 1100-1300 C[2]
Corrosive; releases hydrogen sulfide with water[2]

paras: Strontium sulfide is a white solid that hydrolyses readily in water, giving off hydrogen sulfide and its characteristic odour.[2] In depilatory use the sulfide acts as an alkaline reducing agent on hair keratin.

Depilatories in general are creams or powders that chemically dissolve hair, and their effects are temporary.[3] Ancient depilatory pastes used lime, ash and arsenic sulfide (orpiment) and were highly caustic; sulfide and later thioglycolate products were part of the move toward gentler formulations.[3]

No modern human clinical trials were found. Historical laboratory work includes a 1952 study of the depth to which strontium sulfide depilatories act and a 1953 study of strontium sulfide depilation of rat skin and the effect of lanolin on depilated skin.[4][1]

Strontium sulfide carries hazard statements for causing severe skin burns and eye damage and for being harmful if swallowed.[2] Chemical hair removers as a category can cause skin inflammation, minor burns and folliculitis.[3]
